lessons.title: Water Requirements at Different Growth Stages
lessons.body: Soybeans need different amounts of water at each stage of growth. From planting to emergence, the seed needs enough moisture to swell and sprout, but not so much that it rots. A light irrigation of 15-20 mm after planting is enough if the soil is dry. During the vegetative stage (from emergence to flowering), the plant grows leaves and roots. It uses about 3-4 mm of water per day. In dry conditions, you may need to irrigate every 7-10 days with 25-30 mm. The most critical stage is flowering and pod formation. Water stress now can cut yields by 50% or more. The plant needs 5-6 mm per day. If rainfall is low, irrigate every 5-7 days with 30-35 mm. During pod fill, water helps fill the seeds. Too little water causes small, shriveled beans. Aim for 4-5 mm per day. As the plant matures and leaves turn yellow, water needs drop to 2-3 mm per day. Stop irrigation once pods are full and leaves start dropping to avoid mold. In Africa, where rains can be unpredictable, knowing these stages helps you plan. For example, in Nigeria's Guinea Savannah, soybean flowering often coincides with a dry spell in August. A farmer with a small pump can save the crop by applying 30 mm at that time. Use a rain gauge or a simple tin can to measure rainfall. If you get less than 25 mm in a week, consider irrigation. Remember, soybeans are more drought-tolerant than maize, but they still need consistent moisture for good yields. Sandy soils hold less water, so irrigate more often but with less water each time. Clay soils hold more, so you can wait longer but avoid waterlogging. Always check soil moisture by squeezing a handful of soil: if it crumbles, it's too dry; if it forms a ball, it's good; if it drips, it's too wet.

lessons.title: Irrigation Systems: Drip, Sprinkler, Furrow
lessons.body: Choosing the right irrigation system depends on your field size, water source, and budget. Drip irrigation is the most efficient. It delivers water directly to the plant roots through small tubes with emitters. It saves up to 50% water compared to other methods. For soybeans, use drip lines spaced 0.5-0.75 m apart, with emitters every 30 cm. Each emitter releases 2-4 liters per hour. You can run it for 1-2 hours every day or every other day. Drip is good for small plots (up to 1 hectare) and where water is scarce. It also reduces weeds because only the crop gets water. However, drip systems can clog if water is dirty, so use a filter. Sprinkler irrigation mimics rainfall. You can use hand-moved sprinklers or permanent systems. For soybeans, sprinklers should apply 25-30 mm per application. Space sprinklers 12 m apart and run them for 2-3 hours to get that amount. Sprinklers are good for larger fields (2-5 hectares) and sandy soils. But they can spread diseases if leaves stay wet, so irrigate in the morning so leaves dry before evening. Also, wind can cause uneven watering. Furrow irrigation is the cheapest and most common in Africa. You make small channels between crop rows and let water flow. For soybeans, plant on ridges and make furrows 0.5-0.75 m apart. Water flows down the furrow and soaks into the soil. You need a slope of 0.5-2% for water to flow. Apply water until the furrow is full for about 30 minutes, then move to the next. Furrow uses more water (up to 40% loss) and can cause erosion, but it requires no special equipment. In many parts of Africa, farmers use buckets or watering cans for small plots. That is labor-intensive but works for 0.1 hectare. You can also use a treadle pump to lift water from a well or river. No matter the system, always maintain it: check for leaks, clean filters, and repair broken parts quickly. The best system is one you can afford and manage well.

lessons.title: Scheduling Irrigation Based on Soil Moisture
lessons.body: Irrigating at the right time is as important as how much you apply. You don't want to guess; you want to know when the soil is dry. The simplest tool is your hand. Dig 15 cm into the soil near the plant roots. Take a handful and squeeze it. If it forms a ball that holds together but doesn't drip, the moisture is good. If it crumbles, it's too dry and you need to irrigate. If it drips water, it's too wet and you should wait. Do this test every 2-3 days during flowering and pod fill. Another low-cost tool is a soil moisture meter. You can buy a simple probe for $20-50. It gives a reading of wet, moist, or dry. Insert it 15-20 cm deep at several spots in the field. If most spots read dry, irrigate. For more precision, use a tensiometer. It measures how tightly water is held in the soil. Install it at 30 cm depth. When the reading is above 50 centibars (cb), it's time to irrigate. Below 30 cb, soil is wet enough. Tensiometers cost $50-100 but last for years. You can also use the feel method with a shovel: dig a small hole, feel the soil at 15 cm and 30 cm. If both are dry, irrigate. For soybean, the critical times to check are: just after planting, at flowering, and at pod fill. In these stages, don't let soil moisture drop below 50% of field capacity. In sandy soils, check more often because they dry quickly. In clay soils, check less often but be careful not to overwater. A simple rule: if you get less than 25 mm of rain in a week, check soil moisture. If dry, apply 25-30 mm of water. Keep a record of rainfall and irrigation dates in a notebook. This helps you learn your field's pattern. In Africa, where rains are erratic, scheduling is key to saving water and getting a good harvest. You can also use a rain gauge made from a tin can to measure rainfall. Place it in an open area and check daily. If you know a dry spell is coming, irrigate before the soil gets too dry. This reduces stress on the plants.

lessons.title: Drainage Management to Prevent Waterlogging
lessons.body: Soybeans hate waterlogged soil. Too much water in the root zone stops the roots from taking up nutrients and can cause root rot. Waterlogging for just 3-5 days during flowering can cut yields by 30-50%. In Africa, heavy rains can flood fields, especially in low-lying areas or on clay soils. To prevent this, you need good drainage. The first step is to make raised beds or ridges. Plant soybeans on ridges 20-30 cm high. This keeps the roots above the water table. If you use furrow irrigation, make sure the furrows drain well. At the end of each furrow, dig a shallow ditch to carry excess water away. For flat fields, create a system of open drains. Dig ditches 30-50 cm deep and 30 cm wide along the edges and through the field every 10-15 meters. These drains collect surface water and lead it to a lower area or a stream. In small plots, you can use a spade to make shallow channels. Another method is subsoiling. If you have a tractor, use a subsoiler to break up compacted soil layers 30-40 cm deep. This allows water to soak in faster. For farmers without tractors, use a fork jembe or hoe to loosen soil. Also, add organic matter like compost or manure. It improves soil structure and helps water drain. If your field is in a valley, consider making a diversion ditch on the uphill side to redirect runoff. In areas with heavy rains, plant on the contour (across the slope) to slow water flow. Check your field after every heavy rain. If you see standing water for more than a day, improve drainage immediately. You can also plant cover crops like cowpea or mucuna in the off-season to improve soil. Remember, soybeans are more sensitive to waterlogging than maize. If you see yellowing leaves and stunted growth, it might be waterlogging. Act fast: open drains and avoid irrigating until the soil dries. In the dry season, you can use the same drains for irrigation if needed. Good drainage also reduces disease like root rot and charcoal rot. So invest in drainage before planting.

lessons.title: Drought Stress Mitigation Techniques
lessons.body: Drought can hit soybeans at any stage, but flowering and pod fill are the most damaging. When plants don't get enough water, they wilt, leaves curl, and pods fail to fill. But you can reduce the damage. First, choose drought-tolerant varieties. In Africa, varieties like 'TGX' lines from IITA are bred for drought tolerance. Ask your extension officer for recommendations. Second, plant early when rains are reliable. If you plant with the first rains, the crop has more time to grow before a dry spell. Third, use mulch. Spread crop residues like maize stalks or grass between rows. A 5 cm layer of mulch reduces evaporation by up to 70%. It keeps soil cool and moist. You can also use plastic mulch, but it's expensive. Fourth, practice conservation tillage. Don't plow too much; leave residues on the surface. This helps water infiltrate and reduces runoff. Fifth, if you have irrigation, apply water at critical stages. Even one good irrigation at flowering can save the crop. If you don't have irrigation, you can use a bottle drip system: bury a plastic bottle with small holes near the plant roots and fill it with water. It slowly releases water. For larger areas, use a treadle pump to lift water from a well. Sixth, reduce plant density. If drought is expected, plant fewer seeds per hectare. Plants will have more water each. Seventh, control weeds. Weeds compete for water. Keep the field clean. Eighth, apply potassium fertilizer. Potassium helps plants regulate water. Use 50 kg/ha of muriate of potash. Ninth, if drought hits, you can spray a kaolin clay solution on leaves. It reflects sunlight and reduces water loss. Mix 30 g of kaolin per liter of water and spray. Tenth, harvest early if drought is severe. If pods are filling but plants are dying, you can harvest and use the beans for seed or feed. Don't wait for total loss. Finally, keep records. Note when drought occurs and how you responded. This helps you plan next season. In Africa, climate change is making droughts more common, so these techniques are essential. Even small actions can make a big difference.

lessons.title: Water Conservation Practices
lessons.body: Water is precious, especially in Africa where rainfall is often scarce or unpredictable. Conserving water means getting more crop per drop. Start with your soil. Add organic matter like compost, manure, or crop residues. Every 1% increase in soil organic matter can hold an extra 20,000 liters of water per hectare. So make compost from kitchen waste, animal dung, and crop residues. Apply 5-10 tons per hectare before planting. Mulching is another key practice. Cover the soil with a 5-10 cm layer of dry grass, straw, or leaves. This reduces evaporation, keeps soil temperature stable, and suppresses weeds. You can also use living mulch like cowpea or groundnut between soybean rows, but be careful not to compete for water. Next, improve your irrigation method. If you use furrow, convert to surge irrigation: apply water in pulses (on and off) to reduce runoff and deep percolation. For sprinklers, irrigate early morning or late evening when evaporation is low. Avoid irrigating on windy days. For drip, use timers or check emitters regularly to avoid overwatering. Harvest rainwater. Build small dams, ponds, or tanks to catch runoff from roofs and fields. A 10,000-liter tank can irrigate 0.1 hectare for a week. You can also dig trenches or swales along the contour to capture rainwater. These are shallow ditches that hold water and let it soak in. In dry areas, use zai pits: dig planting holes 20-30 cm deep and wide, fill with manure, and plant. The pits capture water. Another practice is to reduce tillage. No-till or minimum tillage leaves residues on the surface, which improves water infiltration and reduces evaporation. If you use a plow, don't overdo it. Also, fix leaks in your irrigation system. A single dripping emitter can waste 20 liters per day. Check pipes, joints, and emitters weekly. Train your family or workers on water-saving habits. For example, use a bucket instead of a hose to water seedlings. Finally, plant drought-tolerant varieties and adjust planting dates to match rainfall. In many parts of Africa, the rainy season is getting shorter, so every drop counts. By combining these practices, you can reduce water use by 30-50% while maintaining yields. Remember, conservation is not just for dry times; it's a year-round habit.

quiz.q: At which growth stage do soybeans need the most water?
quiz.explanation: Water stress during flowering and pod formation can reduce yields by 50% or more.

quiz.q: How much water per day do soybeans need during flowering?
quiz.explanation: During flowering, soybeans need about 5-6 mm of water per day.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to measure rainfall?
options: B) Rain gauge or tin can
quiz.explanation: A rain gauge or a simple tin can placed in an open area can measure rainfall.

quiz.q: Which soil type holds less water, requiring more frequent irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils have large pores and drain quickly, so they hold less water.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for drip lines in soybean?
quiz.explanation: Drip lines for soybeans are typically spaced 0.5-0.75 m apart.

quiz.q: Which irrigation system is the most water-efficient?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the roots and can save up to 50% water.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of sprinkler irrigation?
options: B) Can spread diseases if leaves stay wet
D) Only works on clay soils
quiz.explanation: Sprinklers wet the leaves, which can promote fungal diseases if not timed properly.

quiz.q: What slope is needed for furrow irrigation?
quiz.explanation: A slope of 0.5-2% allows water to flow evenly without causing erosion.

quiz.q: What is the hand feel method used for?
quiz.explanation: Squeezing a handful of soil can indicate if it's too dry, good, or too wet.

quiz.q: At what tensiometer reading should you irrigate?
quiz.explanation: A reading above 50 centibars indicates the soil is dry and needs irrigation.

quiz.q: How deep should you dig to check soil moisture by hand?
quiz.explanation: Checking at 15 cm depth gives a good indication of moisture in the root zone.

quiz.q: What is a critical time to check soil moisture for soybeans?
quiz.explanation: Flowering is a critical stage where water stress severely reduces yield.

quiz.q: What is a sign of waterlogged soil?
quiz.explanation: Standing water for more than a day indicates poor drainage and waterlogging.

quiz.q: How high should ridges be to prevent waterlogging?
quiz.explanation: Ridges 20-30 cm high keep the root zone above the water table.

quiz.q: What is a diversion ditch used for?
options: B) To redirect runoff away from the field
quiz.explanation: A diversion ditch on the uphill side redirects runoff that could flood the field.

quiz.q: How does organic matter help with drainage?
quiz.explanation: Organic matter improves soil structure, allowing better water infiltration and drainage.

quiz.q: Which crop is more sensitive to waterlogging?
quiz.explanation: Soybeans are more sensitive to waterlogging than maize.

quiz.q: What is a drought-tolerant soybean variety mentioned?
quiz.explanation: TGX lines from IITA are bred for drought tolerance.

quiz.q: How much can mulch reduce evaporation?
quiz.explanation: A 5 cm layer of mulch can reduce evaporation by up to 70%.

quiz.q: What is a bottle drip system?
options: B) A plastic bottle with holes buried near roots
quiz.explanation: A buried plastic bottle with small holes slowly releases water to plant roots.

quiz.q: Which nutrient helps plants regulate water?
quiz.explanation: Potassium helps plants regulate water and cope with drought stress.

quiz.q: What is kaolin clay spray used for?
quiz.explanation: Kaolin clay reflects sunlight and reduces water loss from leaves.

quiz.q: How much extra water can 1% increase in soil organic matter hold per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Every 1% increase in organic matter can hold an extra 20,000 liters of water per hectare.

quiz.q: What is surge irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Surge irrigation applies water in on-and-off pulses to reduce runoff.

quiz.q: When is the best time to irrigate to reduce evaporation?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Irrigating early morning or late evening reduces water loss to evaporation.

quiz.q: What are zai pits?
options: B) Planting holes that capture water
quiz.explanation: Zai pits are planting holes filled with manure that capture and hold water.

quiz.q: How much water can a dripping emitter waste per day?
quiz.explanation: A single dripping emitter can waste up to 20 liters of water per day.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of no-till farming for water conservation?
options: C) Leaves residues that improve infiltration
quiz.explanation: No-till leaves crop residues on the surface, improving water infiltration and reducing evaporation.

quiz.q: What is a swale?
options: B) A shallow ditch on contour to capture water
quiz.explanation: Swales are shallow ditches dug along the contour to capture and infiltrate rainwater.

quiz.q: By how much can combining water conservation practices reduce water use?
quiz.explanation: Combining practices like mulching, drip irrigation, and rainwater harvesting can reduce water use by 30-50%.
